This setup can leverage Category 6a (Cat 6a) or Category 7 (Cat 7) cables, which can support 10Gbps over longer distances than their predecessors. However, for our 100Gbps target, these cables must be kept under a strict distance limitation—generally around 30 meters for optimal performance. Achieving this requires sophisticated signaling methods, such as pulse amplitude modulation (PAM4), which condenses data into a more efficient format to push through the available bandwidth. It's also important to consider the environmental factors that may affect performance; higher frequencies tend to be more susceptible to interference and attenuation. Therefore, ensuring proper installation practices, such as minimizing bends and maintaining solid connections, is vital. While the upfront costs and infrastructure upgrade may seem hefty compared to fiber optics, which are the preferred medium for such high-speed applications, the flexibility of copper networks can make it a viable option in certain scenarios, especially for shorter distances in data centers or enterprise settings. Satellite signals are very much more subject to noise because they get huge amounts of attenuation over the massive distances they're sent (and wide distribution). Terrestrial signals are less prone to this and have stronger signals, but they're subject to a great deal of reflection and instantaneous noise. They implement not dissimilar techniques but they come at it from a very different objective to deal with very different environments. Importantly, the chips are optimised to fixed function. Making the processing be more flexible means making them more complex. Additionally, if you add components for dealing with driving the satellite LNB, you're spending money and if it's not going to be used, that's money for nothing.
